claim: 1215 amphibian species are being traded, representing 17% of all amphibian species.
source: We show that 1215 species are being traded (17% of amphibian species), almost three times previous recorded numbers
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by data from multiple sources analyzed in the study.

claim: The number of amphibian species in trade is almost three times previous recorded numbers.
source: We show that 1215 species are being traded (17% of amphibian species), almost three times previous recorded numbers
evidence: The abstract compares the current findings to previous studies, indicating a substantial increase.

claim: 345 traded amphibian species are threatened.
source: We show that 1215 species are being traded (17% of amphibian species), almost three times previous recorded numbers, 345 are threatened, and 100 Data Deficient or unassessed.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of threatened species in trade based on the study's analysis.

claim: 100 traded amphibian species are Data Deficient or unassessed.
source: We show that 1215 species are being traded (17% of amphibian species), almost three times previous recorded numbers, 345 are threatened, and 100 Data Deficient or unassessed.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this number based on IUCN assessment data.

claim: 42% of traded amphibians are taken from the wild.
source: sources indicate 42% of amphibians are taken from the wild
evidence: The abstract states this percentage based on analysis of trade data sources.

claim: Newly described amphibian species can be rapidly traded with a mean time lag of 6.5 years.
source: Newly described species can be rapidly traded (mean time lag of 6.5 years), including threatened and unassessed species.
evidence: The abstract reports this finding based on temporal analysis of species description dates and trade appearance.

claim: Traded species origin hotspots include South America, China, and Central Africa.
source: Traded species origin hotspots include South America, China, and Central Africa
evidence: The abstract identifies these geographic hotspots based on spatial analysis of traded species origins.

claim: All Aichi biodiversity targets have been failed to be met at the close of the 'decade of biodiversity'.
source: At the close of a 'decade of biodiversity', we have failed to meet any of the Aichi targets designed to safeguard biodiversity (CBD, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to CBD, 2020.

claim: Unsustainable wildlife exploitation is an important driver of biodiversity loss.
source: One important driver of biodiversity loss is unsustainable wildlife exploitation (IPBES, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to IPBES, 2019.

claim: Amphibians and reptiles are among the most frequently traded animals.
source: Gaps in trade regulations in terms of species covered by international regulation such as by the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) leave groups like amphibians and reptiles among the most frequently traded animals (Herrel and van der Meijden, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Herrel and van der Meijden, 2014.

claim: Only 8.3% of reptile species are under CITES regulations yet over 36% are in trade.
source: Marshall et al., 2020, highlighted the discrepancy in protection within the reptile trade, with only 8.3% under CITES regulations yet over 36% in trade and over 70% of individuals from some taxa (e.g., lizards) harvested from the wild (Marshall et al., 2020; Uetz et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Marshall et al., 2020 and Uetz et al., 2021.

claim: Over 70% of individuals from some reptile taxa (e.g., lizards) are harvested from the wild.
source: Marshall et al., 2020, highlighted the discrepancy in protection within the reptile trade, with only 8.3% under CITES regulations yet over 36% in trade and over 70% of individuals from some taxa (e.g., lizards) harvested from the wild (Marshall et al., 2020; Uetz et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Marshall et al., 2020 and Uetz et al., 2021.

claim: 87% of individual Southeast Asian newts are wild collected.
source: The need for a complete assessment of amphibian species in trade, their origins, and where native populations are at risk is emphasised by targeted studies revealing high rates (87% of individual Southeast Asian newts) of wild collection (Rowley et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rowley et al., 2016.

claim: Only 2.4% of all known amphibian species are listed under CITES regulation.
source: Despite experiencing similar pressures to reptiles and greater sensitivity to perturbations (Stuart et al., 2004), amphibians are one of the least protected taxa under CITES regulation with only 2.4% of all known species listed (second only to fish at 0.46%: http://www.fishbase.org/home.htm)
evidence: This claim is stated in the text with reference to Stuart et al., 2004 for context on pressures.

claim: Fish have the lowest CITES protection at 0.46% of species listed.
source: amphibians are one of the least protected taxa under CITES regulation with only 2.4% of all known species listed (second only to fish at 0.46%: http://www.fishbase.org/home.htm)
evidence: This claim is stated in the text with a reference to fishbase.org.

claim: Amphibians show faster population declines than any other vertebrate group.
source: despite showing faster population declines than any other vertebrate group (Hoffmann et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hoffmann et al., 2010.

claim: Amphibian trade is directly tied to introduced pathogens, invasive species, and wildlife collection.
source: Often dubbed canaries in the coal-mine amphibians are sensitive to a myriad of anthropogenic stressors: pollution (Blaustein et al., 2003), habitat loss (Stuart et al., 2004), atmospheric changes (Blaustein et al., 2003), introduced pathogens (Lips, 2016), invasive species (Bellard et al., 2016), wildlife collection (Phimmachak et al., 2012), and agricultural chemicals (Trudeau et al., 2020); such stressors are exacerbated by amphibians' frequently small distributions and naturally fluctuating populations (Nori et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2012). Amphibian trade is directly tied to the last three stressors.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated with multiple supporting citations for the various stressors.

claim: Trade can enable pathogen spread in amphibians.
source: Trade can enable pathogen spread (O'Hanlon et al., 2018), which has facilitated devastating amphibian species loss (Scheele et al., 2019; but see Lambert et al., 2020, for concerns over the number of species).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to O'Hanlon et al., 2018, Scheele et al., 2019, and Lambert et al., 2020.

claim: Pathogen spread has facilitated devastating amphibian species loss.
source: Trade can enable pathogen spread (O'Hanlon et al., 2018), which has facilitated devastating amphibian species loss (Scheele et al., 2019; but see Lambert et al., 2020, for concerns over the number of species).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Scheele et al., 2019, with a note about concerns from Lambert et al., 2020.

claim: Invasive amphibians are often linked to trade.
source: Invasive amphibians (often linked to trade; Lockwood et al., 2019; Stringham and Lockwood, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lockwood et al., 2019 and Stringham and Lockwood, 2018.

claim: A recent literature assessment found 443 amphibian species in pet trade.
source: A recent literature assessment of amphibian pet trade found 443 traded species (Mohanty and Measey, 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mohanty and Measey, 2019.

claim: The online search examined 139 amphibian selling websites and retrieved 2766 web pages in the 2020 snapshot.
source: Our online search efforts successfully examined a total of 139 amphibian selling websites and retrieved 2766 web pages to be searched (mean of 19.91 ± 3.95 pages per website; range 1–302).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the data collection process.

claim: The temporal online sample added an additional 4568 pages to the search.
source: Our temporal online sample (2004–2019) added an additional 4568 pages, meaning our complete online species list is based on searches across 7334 pages in total.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the data collection process.

claim: 575 species were detected in the Online trade data source.
source: resulting in a total of 575 species detected in the Online trade.
evidence: This is a finding from the online search methodology.

claim: 909 species were detected across CITES, LEMIS, and Online trade data sources combined.
source: Overall, the three data sources (Online trade, LEMIS, and CITES trade database) contained 909 species in total (11.06% of the 8212 total described amphibian species)
evidence: This is a finding from combining the three contemporary data sources.

claim: LEMIS had the most species (587 species, 31% unique) among the three contemporary data sources.
source: of which LEMIS had the most (587 species, 31% unique), followed by Online trade (575 species, 30% unique) then CITES (137 species, 4% unique).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the three contemporary data sources.

claim: 99.6% of the trade detected was commercial with only 0.4% non-commercial.
source: Most of this trade was commercial (99.6%) with only 0.4% non-commercial.
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing the purpose of trade in the data sources.

claim: Anurans dominated the trade with 729 species.
source: Unsurprisingly, anurans (729 species) dominated the trade, followed by salamanders (162 species) and caecilians (18 species).
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing the taxonomic composition of traded species.

claim: 157 threatened species were detected in trade based on the three trade inventories.
source: Based on these three trade inventories, a total of 157 species were threatened (i.e., listed as Vulnerable (VU, EN, CR) or worse on the IUCN Redlist), 27 Data Deficient, and 39 unassessed, and the remainder Least Concern (Figure 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1.

claim: 95% of species in trade in CITES have a CITES appendix listing.
source: Whilst the majority of species in trade in CITES have a CITES appendix (95%), this is not the case for species detected via LEMIS (14%) or online searches (16%).
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing CITES appendix coverage across data sources.

claim: Only 14% of species detected via LEMIS have a CITES appendix listing.
source: Whilst the majority of species in trade in CITES have a CITES appendix (95%), this is not the case for species detected via LEMIS (14%) or online searches (16%).
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing CITES appendix coverage across data sources.

claim: Only 16% of species detected via online searches have a CITES appendix listing.
source: Whilst the majority of species in trade in CITES have a CITES appendix (95%), this is not the case for species detected via LEMIS (14%) or online searches (16%).
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing CITES appendix coverage across data sources.

claim: 47% of species in trade via CITES are threatened according to the IUCN.
source: In terms of the degree of threat, 47% of species in trade via CITES are threatened according to the IUCN and 12% are unlisted by the IUCN, whereas this is lower for LEMIS (24%; 5%) and Online (23%; 6%).
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing threat status across data sources.

claim: 24% of species in trade via LEMIS are threatened according to the IUCN.
source: In terms of the degree of threat, 47% of species in trade via CITES are threatened according to the IUCN and 12% are unlisted by the IUCN, whereas this is lower for LEMIS (24%; 5%) and Online (23%; 6%).
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing threat status across data sources.

claim: 23% of species in trade via Online searches are threatened according to the IUCN.
source: In terms of the degree of threat, 47% of species in trade via CITES are threatened according to the IUCN and 12% are unlisted by the IUCN, whereas this is lower for LEMIS (24%; 5%) and Online (23%; 6%).
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing threat status across data sources.

claim: Of the 69,771,677 amphibians imported into the USA recorded by LEMIS, 57.2% are listed as captive sourced.
source: Of the 69,771,677 amphibians imported into the USA, recorded by LEMIS, 57.2% (39,921,289) are listed as captive sourced, leaving 42.3% (29,522,128) as originating from the wild (the remaining 0.47%, 328,260, classed as other or with an ambiguous source).
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing LEMIS data on source of traded individuals.

claim: 42.3% of amphibians imported into the USA recorded by LEMIS originate from the wild.
source: Of the 69,771,677 amphibians imported into the USA, recorded by LEMIS, 57.2% (39,921,289) are listed as captive sourced, leaving 42.3% (29,522,128) as originating from the wild (the remaining 0.47%, 328,260, classed as other or with an ambiguous source).
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing LEMIS data on source of traded individuals.

claim: 254 out of 259 imported genera are impacted by wild capture.
source: The vast majority of imported genera are impacted by wild capture (254/259) with 141 genera exclusively wild-sourced
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing LEMIS data at the genus level.

claim: 141 genera are exclusively wild-sourced according to LEMIS data.
source: The vast majority of imported genera are impacted by wild capture (254/259) with 141 genera exclusively wild-sourced; five genera are fully sourced from captive operations (Peltophryne, Ranitomeya, Calyptocephalella, Cryptophyllobates, Samandrella; Figure 3—figure supplements 1–6).
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing LEMIS data at the genus level, supported by figure supplements.

claim: Five genera are fully sourced from captive operations: Peltophryne, Ranitomeya, Calyptocephalella, Cryptophyllobates, Samandrella.
source: five genera are fully sourced from captive operations (Peltophryne, Ranitomeya, Calyptocephalella, Cryptophyllobates, Samandrella; Figure 3—figure supplements 1–6).
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing LEMIS data at the genus level, supported by figure supplements.

claim: On average 84.2% of each genus's individuals come from the wild.
source: On average 84.2% of each genera's individuals come from the wild, and a per genera median of 100% is likely driven by the large number of genera exclusively taken from the wild but in much lower volumes
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing LEMIS data at the genus level.

claim: The CITES trade has remained relatively consistent over time between 2000 and 2020 at around 50 species a year with a gradual increase.
source: Whilst the CITES trade has remained relatively consistent over time between 2000 and 2020 at around 50 species a year with a gradual increase of species, LEMIS shows an increase up to 2014 (the limit of available data) at 310 species (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from temporal analysis of CITES data, supported by Figure 3A.

claim: LEMIS shows an increase in traded species up to 2014 at 310 species.
source: Whilst the CITES trade has remained relatively consistent over time between 2000 and 2020 at around 50 species a year with a gradual increase of species, LEMIS shows an increase up to 2014 (the limit of available data) at 310 species (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from temporal analysis of LEMIS data, supported by Figure 3A.

claim: 38 species described since 1999 appeared in trade based on the three inventories.
source: Thirty-eight species described since 1999 (1.38% of the 2747 amphibian species described after 1999; Figure 4A and B) appeared in trade based on our three inventories
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing newly described species in trade, supported by Figure 4.

claim: 30 newly described species had a mean time lag of 6.5±0.78 years between species description and appearance in trade.
source: Eight only appeared in the 2019 snapshot, so are discounted from time lag calculations, leaving 30 species with connected trade years and a mean time lag of 6.5±0.78 years between species description and appearance in the trade.
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing the time lag between description and trade appearance.

claim: One newly described species was in trade the year after it was described.
source: One species was in trade the year after it was described, but four were in trade in the second year, four in the third year, and seven within 4–5 years (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing the time lag between description and trade appearance, supported by Figure 4C.

claim: English and German language searches detected the most species (293, 289 respectively).
source: English and German detected the most species by far (293, 289), and each also contained the highest rates of unique species (81, 97).
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing online search results by language.

claim: English and German language searches contained the highest rates of unique species (81, 97 respectively).
source: English and German detected the most species by far (293, 289), and each also contained the highest rates of unique species (81, 97).
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing online search results by language.

claim: Combining all sources yielded 1500 amphibian species in trade before synonyms were removed.
source: Combining all sources yielded a total of 1500 amphibian species in trade before synonyms were removed, and 1215 once synonyms were removed, equivalent to 17% of amphibian species.
evidence: This is a finding from combining all five data sources.

claim: Up to 413 species are used for meat.
source: The 1215 species included up to 413 species used for meat (though a significant number were largely local consumption based on IUCN assessments)
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing the purposes of trade across all data sources.

claim: 805 species are traded as pets.
source: 805 species as pets (though six are from separate lists: one from Germany; Altherr and Lameter, 2020; five from Asia; Choquette et al., 2020)
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing the purposes of trade across all data sources, with citations for additional lists.

claim: 122 species are used as medicine or in pharmacological research.
source: 122 species used as medicine or in pharmacological research
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing the purposes of trade across all data sources.

claim: 664 species are imported for research or breeding facilities (including zoos and aquaria).
source: 664 species imported for research or breeding facilities (including zoos and aquaria)
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing the purposes of trade across all data sources.

claim: 22% of species in trade are threatened (Vulnerable or worse).
source: In total, 22% of species in trade are threatened (i.e., Vulnerable or worse, 28% when Near-Threatened are also considered)
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing threat status of all traded species.

claim: 28% of species in trade are threatened when Near-Threatened are also considered.
source: In total, 22% of species in trade are threatened (i.e., Vulnerable or worse, 28% when Near-Threatened are also considered)
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing threat status of all traded species.

claim: CITES covers only 12% of all traded amphibian species (151/1215).
source: In terms of coverage of species for each type of trade by CITES (12% overall 151/1215)
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing CITES coverage of all traded species.

claim: CITES covers only 5% of species used for meat.
source: this varied from 5% of species used for meat, to 16% of those used for pets or 18% for medicine, and 16% of those in research.
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing CITES coverage by trade purpose.

claim: Global export of frog legs is dominated by Indonesia at 8,005,997 kg in 2008–2009.
source: Commercial trade of amphibians for meat is also shown to be from Asia using the United Nations Commodity Trade Statistics Database (UN Comtrade: https://comtrade.un.org/data/) which shows that global export of frog legs is dominated by Indonesia (at 8,005,997 kg in 2008–2009 alone), followed by China, Vietnam, and other Asian nations with the dominant markets in France, Belgium, and the USA
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing UN Comtrade data on frog leg exports.

claim: 94 cases out of 159 extinct and potentially extinct amphibian species from the 2008 Global Amphibian Assessment are at least partially attributed to Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd).
source: To date, 94 cases out of the 159 extinct and potentially extinct species from the 2008 Global Amphibian Assessment are at least partially attributed to Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) (MacCulloch, 2008; Picco and Collins, 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to MacCulloch, 2008 and Picco and Collins, 2008.

claim: Bd is likely responsible for up to 500 species declines.
source: suggestions that Bd is likely to be responsible for up to 500 species declines (Scheele et al., 2019; but see Lambert et al., 2020 for discussion on the 500+ estimate).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Scheele et al., 2019, with a note about discussion in Lambert et al., 2020.

claim: Rates of Bd in live exports can be over 60% of individuals.
source: Rates of Bd in live exports can be high (over 60% of individuals), with studies linking the spread of Bd and Bsal to the trade of live animals in the pet trade (Fitzpatrick et al., 2018; Kriger and Hero, 2009; Yuan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fitzpatrick et al., 2018, Kriger and Hero, 2009, and Yuan et al., 2018.

claim: Mortality during transit and transport can be as high as 72% in some studies.
source: Furthermore, quantitative analysis of the volumes of species in trade often relies on import data (e.g., LEMIS) and ignores mortality during transit and transport, which has been shown to be as high as 72% in some studies (Ashley et al., 2014), with mortality in amphibians higher than all other groups (45% within 10 days of confiscation).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ashley et al., 2014.

claim: Mortality in amphibians is higher than all other groups at 45% within 10 days of confiscation.
source: Furthermore, quantitative analysis of the volumes of species in trade often relies on import data (e.g., LEMIS) and ignores mortality during transit and transport, which has been shown to be as high as 72% in some studies (Ashley et al., 2014), with mortality in amphibians higher than all other groups (45% within 10 days of confiscation).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ashley et al., 2014.

claim: CITES does not include 97.5% of amphibian species.
source: Because of novelty dynamics in trade and changing taxonomy, CITES appears an inadequate tool to describe taxonomic or spatial trade patterns; CITES does not include 97.5% of amphibian species
evidence: This is calculated from the finding that only 2.4% of amphibian species are listed under CITES.

claim: The World Customs Organization still fails to list species data in exports.
source: Despite the impact of trade, the World Customs Organization still fails to list species data in exports – only basic data is needed to legally export most amphibians, providing no species-specific information to enable trade monitoring.
evidence: This is a statement about current regulatory practices.

claim: One in ten traded species are highly threatened (11% of species Endangered or Critically Endangered).
source: We show 22% of the 1215 species in trade are threatened (i.e., IUCN Redlist status of Vulnerable or worse), and a further 8% remain unassessed or Data Deficient. One in ten traded species are already highly threatened (11% of species Endangered or Critically Endangered).
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing threat status of all traded species.

claim: 8% of traded species remain unassessed or Data Deficient.
source: We show 22% of the 1215 species in trade are threatened (i.e., IUCN Redlist status of Vulnerable or worse), and a further 8% remain unassessed or Data Deficient.
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing threat status of all traded species.

claim: Traded populations of mammals, birds, and reptiles show abundance declines of 62% (95% CI 20–82%).
source: A recent meta-analysis on how trade impacts wild populations was unable to generate an estimate on amphibians because of a lack of standardised studies, but revealed abundance declines of 62% (95% CI 20–82%) in traded populations of mammals, birds, and reptiles (Morton et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Morton et al., 2021.

claim: Different data sources detected different species in trade, and no single source is sufficient to detect all species traded.
source: Comparisons reveal that different sources detected different species in the trade, and no single source is sufficient to detect all species traded (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the five data sources, supported by Figure 6.

claim: The online search used Google and Bing search engines to discover contemporary websites selling amphibians.
source: We used Google and Bing search engines to discover contemporary websites selling amphibians.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the data collection process.

claim: The study targeted amphibian selling websites in six languages: English, French, German, Japanese, Portuguese, and Spanish.
source: We targeted amphibian selling websites in English, French, German, Japanese, Portuguese, and Spanish, to cover the largest herpetofauna pet trade markets.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the data collection process.

claim: The study reviewed 1069 websites in total, with 139 suitable for searching.
source: The new URLs located in the simpler search were reviewed bringing the total reviewed websites to 1069 and the suitable websites to 139 (906 excluded because they did not sell amphibians, 13 specifically stated no automated searching of the website, 6 were duplicates, and the remaining 5 had issues with access).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the data collection process.

claim: The study used AmphibiaWeb data as the taxonomic backbone.
source: We used species data from AmphibiaWeb as our taxonomic backbone (AmphibiaWeb, 2020; https://amphibiaweb.org/amphib_names.txt; accessed 2020-08-29; 2).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the taxonomic reference used.

claim: 99.9% of trade described in LEMIS 2000–2014 is not from seizure and enters the USA.
source: Of the trade described in LEMIS 2000–2014, and constituting/representing single individual animals, 99.9% is not from seizure and enters the USA (69,688,337/69,771,677)
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing LEMIS data.

claim: 99.6% of amphibians imported into the USA recorded by LEMIS are for commercial purposes.
source: the vast majority is for commercial purposes (69,492,478/69,771,677; 99.6%).
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing LEMIS data on trade purpose.

claim: Amphibians are sensitive to pollution.
source: Often dubbed canaries in the coal-mine amphibians are sensitive to a myriad of anthropogenic stressors: pollution (Blaustein et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Blaustein et al., 2003.

claim: Amphibians are sensitive to habitat loss.
source: Often dubbed canaries in the coal-mine amphibians are sensitive to a myriad of anthropogenic stressors: pollution (Blaustein et al., 2003), habitat loss (Stuart et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stuart et al., 2004.

claim: Amphibians are sensitive to atmospheric changes.
source: Often dubbed canaries in the coal-mine amphibians are sensitive to a myriad of anthropogenic stressors: pollution (Blaustein et al., 2003), habitat loss (Stuart et al., 2004), atmospheric changes (Blaustein et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Blaustein et al., 2003.

claim: Amphibians are sensitive to introduced pathogens.
source: Often dubbed canaries in the coal-mine amphibians are sensitive to a myriad of anthropogenic stressors: pollution (Blaustein et al., 2003), habitat loss (Stuart et al., 2004), atmospheric changes (Blaustein et al., 2003), introduced pathogens (Lips, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lips, 2016.

claim: Amphibians are sensitive to invasive species.
source: Often dubbed canaries in the coal-mine amphibians are sensitive to a myriad of anthropogenic stressors: pollution (Blaustein et al., 2003), habitat loss (Stuart et al., 2004), atmospheric changes (Blaustein et al., 2003), introduced pathogens (Lips, 2016), invasive species (Bellard et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bellard et al., 2016.

claim: Amphibians are sensitive to wildlife collection.
source: Often dubbed canaries in the coal-mine amphibians are sensitive to a myriad of anthropogenic stressors: pollution (Blaustein et al., 2003), habitat loss (Stuart et al., 2004), atmospheric changes (Blaustein et al., 2003), introduced pathogens (Lips, 2016), invasive species (Bellard et al., 2016), wildlife collection (Phimmachak et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Phimmachak et al., 2012.

claim: Amphibians are sensitive to agricultural chemicals.
source: Often dubbed canaries in the coal-mine amphibians are sensitive to a myriad of anthropogenic stressors: pollution (Blaustein et al., 2003), habitat loss (Stuart et al., 2004), atmospheric changes (Blaustein et al., 2003), introduced pathogens (Lips, 2016), invasive species (Bellard et al., 2016), wildlife collection (Phimmachak et al., 2012), and agricultural chemicals (Trudeau et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Trudeau et al., 2020.

claim: Amphibian stressors are exacerbated by frequently small distributions and naturally fluctuating populations.
source: such stressors are exacerbated by amphibians' frequently small distributions and naturally fluctuating populations (Nori et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nori et al., 2018, Luo et al., 2015, and Hu et al., 2012.

claim: Invasive amphibians can be vectors for pathogen spread.
source: Invasive amphibians (often linked to trade; Lockwood et al., 2019; Stringham and Lockwood, 2018) can be vectors for pathogen spread (Bienentreu and Lesbarrères, 2020; Feldmeier et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bienentreu and Lesbarrères, 2020 and Feldmeier et al., 2016.

claim: Invasive amphibians can compete with native species for resources such as space and prey.
source: but also can compete with native species for resources such as space and prey (Falaschi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Falaschi et al., 2020.

claim: Humans collect amphibian species for trade, consumption, and medicine on local levels.
source: Wild collection (directly taking animals from the wild) occurs at several scales: on local levels, humans collecting species for trade, consumption, and medicine (Ribas and Poonlaphdecha, 2017; Van Vliet et al., 2017; Onadeko et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ribas and Poonlaphdecha, 2017, Van Vliet et al., 2017, and Onadeko et al., 2011.

claim: Amphibian trade is augmented by demand for pharmaceutical products, pets, and fashion.
source: whereas more widely amphibian trade is augmented by demand for pharmaceutical products, pets, and even fashion (Auliya et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Auliya et al., 2016 and Xiao et al., 2011.

claim: Relying on regulator data can miss critical legal un/under-regulated trade.
source: Previous studies aiming to quantify global patterns of trade have relied upon accessible data (such as CITES and IUCN data; i.e., Scheffers et al., 2019); relying on regulator data can miss critical legal un/under-regulated trade, as evidenced by analysis on reptiles which highlighted the proportion of species in trade fall outside the scope of CITES (Marshall et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Scheffers et al., 2019 and Marshall et al., 2020.

claim: Over 70% of individuals from some lizard taxa are harvested from the wild.
source: Marshall et al., 2020, highlighted the discrepancy in protection within the reptile trade, with only 8.3% under CITES regulations yet over 36% in trade and over 70% of individuals from some taxa (e.g., lizards) harvested from the wild (Marshall et al., 2020; Uetz et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Marshall et al., 2020 and Uetz et al., 2021.

claim: Unregulated harvest from the wild could potentially pose a significant risk to the continued survival of rare or small-ranged species.
source: Whilst trade of wild-collected individuals is not necessarily unsustainable, such a judgement should rely on data, as unregulated harvest from the wild, especially for rare or small-ranged species could potentially pose a significant risk to the continued survival of such populations (Auliya et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Auliya et al., 2016 and represents a logical inference about risk.

claim: Meat trade impacts at least 40 amphibian species annually from Indonesia alone.
